idiom_name: async function + await (Promise.then as the underlying bind)
implementation_notes: A Promise is the language's IO/continuation monad: Promise.resolve is unit and then(onFulfilled) is bind - it flattens a promise returned by the callback instead of nesting it, and a rejection short-circuits the rest of the chain. async/await is the desugared, readable form of the same structure: each await is a then, the async function always returns a promise, and code after an await behaves like a then callback. Use the then form only when building pipelines dynamically from an array of steps or when a library hands you callbacks.
pitfalls: Forgetting to return inside a then callback detaches the step: the chain continues with undefined while the work is still running.
An unhandled rejection terminates modern Node processes and surfaces as an uncaught error in browsers; every chain needs a catch or an awaiting try/catch.
Sequential awaits serialise independent work; combine them with Promise.all/aggregate instead of awaiting one after the other.

variants.name: Promise.then chaining
variants.implementation_notes: The explicit chain form makes monadic bind visible: each callback returns either a plain value or another promise, and then flattens it, so data flows from step to step while rejections skip ahead to the nearest catch. Use it when the pipeline is assembled dynamically (arr.reduce((p, step) => p.then(step), Promise.resolve(x))) or when callbacks come from an API; otherwise async/await is the same structure with better readability and stack behaviour.
variants.code_sketch:
Promise.resolve(userId)
  .then(users.find)               // bind: promise of user
  .then(user => orders.of(user))  // depends on the previous value
  .then(summarize)
  .catch(console.error);
pitfalls: A single catch at the end also swallows programming errors from earlier steps; distinguish expected failures from bugs.
then callbacks lose the surrounding stack; debugging long chains needs rejection hooks or async/await instead.
